\chapter{The Harvest}
\label{ch:ta-the-harvest}
\hlchaptermodality{64}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name paddy, grass, a standing crop, a threshing floor and the harvest in Tamil.}

Complete TA-C64-harvest and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[nel]{\ta{நெல்} (nel) — paddy}

\label{lesson:TA-C64-paddy}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nambikkai} mean, and what did \emph{paṇivu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{நெல்}}
\textbf{\ta{நெல்}} (\emph{nel}) — \textquotedblleft{}paddy\textquotedblright{}.

Rice still in its husk — standing in the \ta{வயல்}, cut, carried, stored, but not yet \ta{அரிசி}. The two words do not trade places: \ta{நெல்} goes into the field and \ta{அரிசி} comes out of the kitchen, and the husking is the border between them.

Kannada \ka{ಭತ್ತ} (\emph{bhatta}) and Telugu \te{వరి} (\emph{vari}) each have their own word for it, so this is one the three do not share.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five field words.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nel}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{nel}, then \emph{arisi}, and say which one the husk is still on
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{நெல்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}paddy\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pul]{\ta{புல்} (pul) — grass}

\label{lesson:TA-C64-grass}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nel} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{புல்}}
\textbf{\ta{புல்}} (\emph{pul}) — \textquotedblleft{}grass\textquotedblright{}.

Grass, of the kind cut and carried home. Kannada makes it \ka{ಹುಲ್ಲು} (\emph{hullu}) — the \emph{p}-for-\emph{h} trade a third time, and by now you can guess a Kannada word before you meet it. Telugu went elsewhere, to \te{గడ్డి} (\emph{gaḍḍi}).

\ta{புல்} and \ta{பல்} sit one mark apart, and the mark is the whole difference: keep the \ta{உ} round and low and the word stays grass. A \ta{பசு} and an \ta{ஆடு} are put out for \ta{புல்}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pul}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{pul}, then \emph{pal}, and hold the two vowels apart
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{புல்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}grass\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[payir]{\ta{பயிர்} (payir) — a standing crop}

\label{lesson:TA-C64-crop}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{pul} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{பயிர்}}
\textbf{\ta{பயிர்}} (\emph{payir}) — \textquotedblleft{}a standing crop\textquotedblright{}.

What is growing in the \ta{வயல்} at this moment, green and still rooted. It is not the \ta{வயல்}, which stays there when nothing is on it, and it is not the \ta{நெல்} in the sack, which has stopped growing.

So the run has three separate things now where English leans on one word: the ground, the standing green, and the grain. Kannada calls the standing green \ka{ಬೆಳೆ} (\emph{beḷe}).

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and the three are carefully apart.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{payir}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vayal}, then \emph{payir}, then \emph{nel}, in that order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{பயிர்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a standing crop\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kaḷam]{\ta{களம்} (kaḷam) — a threshing floor}

\label{lesson:TA-C64-threshing-floor}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{payir} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{களம்}}
\textbf{\ta{களம்}} (\emph{kaḷam}) — \textquotedblleft{}a threshing floor\textquotedblright{}.

The beaten flat ground at the edge of a village where cut \ta{நெல்} is spread, trodden and winnowed. Telugu has the same word as \te{కల్లం} (\emph{kallaṁ}), which makes it old.

It is not \ta{காலம்}, the season word you already have. This one is short at the front and takes the \ta{ள}; \ta{காலம்} opens long and takes the \ta{ல}. One mark and one letter, and they are unrelated.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kaḷam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kaḷam}, then \emph{nel}, and say what is brought to which
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{களம்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a threshing floor\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aṟuvaṭai]{\ta{அறுவடை} (aṟuvaṭai) — the harvest}

\label{lesson:TA-C64-harvest}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kaḷam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{அறுவடை}}
\textbf{\ta{அறுவடை}} (\emph{aṟuvaṭai}) — \textquotedblleft{}the harvest\textquotedblright{}.

The cutting and the gathering together, and the stretch of the year named after them. Kannada \ka{ಸುಗ್ಗಿ} (\emph{suggi}) and Telugu \te{పంట} (\emph{paṇṭa}) each named the same weeks their own way.

The front of it is the reaping, not the \ta{ஆறு} you counted with: this one opens short on \ta{அ} and takes the hard \ta{ற} straight away, where six opens long on \ta{ஆ}. Close together on the page, far apart in the mouth.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the run is closed: paddy, grass, a standing crop, a threshing floor, and the harvest.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{aṟuvaṭai}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{nel}, \emph{pul}, \emph{payir}, \emph{kaḷam}, \emph{aṟuvaṭai}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{அறுவடை} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the harvest\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
